To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

a model that includes the phase changes and the latent heat, and a laser profile that matches the experimental one, are the two most important ingredients for accurate prediction of the melt pool shape in the laser powder bed fusion process.

(a) a well-calibrated purely thermal model, which includes the latent heat, is able to accurately predict the melt pool shape in the laser powder bed fusion process, provided that the laser profile is known; and (b) a simplified model of anisotropic conductivity is able to accurately model the process without any prior knowledge of the laser profile, but with the price of a slightly higher computational complexity.
a purely thermal model is capable of predicting the width, depth, length, and cooling rate of a melt pool with a maximum deviation of 7.3%, if the laser profile is well-calibrated.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of an accurate and efficient model, which is able to predict the shape and cooling rate of the melt pool in laser powder bed fusion, and which can be used for the development of future numerical models for this technology.
the development of a predictive model for the melt pool geometry, and it is based on a physical model that is computationally inexpensive, and therefore suitable for industrial use.
the development of a predictive, yet computationally affordable model for laser powder bed fusion, and the model is validated against experimental results.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a purely thermal model with isotropic conductivity is able to provide a reasonable estimate of the melt pool geometry.

the model, based on the temperature equation including phase changes, is able to predict the melt pool shape with an accuracy of 6.6% (for isotropic thermal conductivity) to 6.5% (for anisotropic thermal conductivity) and that the anisotropy of thermal conductivity, although more predictive than the isotropic model, does not significantly increase the computational complexity of the problem.

a well-calibratable purely thermal model based only on isotropic thermal conductivities is sufficient to predict the quantities of interest with sufficient accuracy, but that the introduction of a simple model for heat material convective effects is beneficial to further increase accuracy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

a purely thermal model based either on an isotropic or an anisotropic conductivity can be used to predict the quantities of interest of the melt pool, with a deviation of less than 7.3%, from the experimental values.

, by using a simple model for heat material transport in the melt pool and a laser profile with an adequate accuracy, the model presented here is able to predict the quantities of interest with a deviation of less than 7% from the experimental results.

the model based on the transient temperature equation, including phase change, is able to predict the quantities of interest with high accuracy, provided that the thermal properties are properly calibrated, and that the model is updated by introducing anisotropy.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a well-calibrating, purely thermal model, based on isotropic conductivity, is able to accurately predict all quantities of interest, including the cooling rate.
, if the laser shape is not measured, the isotropic model can be used to predict the melt pool dimensions, with an error of less than 8% for the quantities of interest.
the model based on isotropy and the double-ellipsoid laser profile is able to predict the quantities of interest with sufficient accuracy.
